Swamp wallaby neonates emerge following a brief gestation of 35 days [tg = 35 days] at the species' typical maternal core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a pregnancy duration that is remarkably short even among macropodids. At birth, the altricial neonate weighs a mere 0.61 grams [Wwb = 0.61 grams], a minuscule mass reflecting the marsupial strategy of a very early parturition followed by an extended period of postnatal development within the pouch. This extremely altricial newborn must immediately crawl from the birth canal to the teat, where it attaches firmly to begin suckling. The entire birthing process, from the initial contractions to the neonatal ascent, is completed within minutes. Despite its diminutive size at delivery, the young is equipped with well-developed forelimbs and a strong jaw musculature that enable this critical first journey. The sustained lactation that follows will transfer the bulk of maternal investment to the developing joey over the subsequent weeks, a phase during which the pouch environment, maintained near 36.5 °C, provides both thermal stability and protection from external threats.

Following several months of continuous suckling within the pouch, the juvenile swamp wallaby achieves a weaning mass of 385 grams [Wwx = 385 grams] when it permanently exits the pouch at around 150 days after birth [tx = around 150 days after birth], a developmental milestone that coincides with the thermal conditions of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] typical of the mother's body temperature. At this point, the joey begins to sample solid vegetation while still supplementing its diet with milk during a gradual transition to nutritional independence. The pouch exit marks an energetically demanding shift for both mother and offspring, as the young animal must now thermoregulate independently and develop functional digestive capabilities to process fibrous plant matter. During the weaning period, maternal investment is heavily concentrated on milk synthesis. Juvenile swamp wallabies continue a steady growth trajectory well after weaning, with females typically attaining their pubertal body mass of 7000 grams [Wwp = 7000 grams] at approximately 638 days after birth [tp = approximately 638 days after birth], a measure taken under the species' active metabolic temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This relatively late onset of sexual maturation reflects the extended period required to achieve a critical body size before initiating reproductive cycling. The time from birth to puberty is considerably longer than the gestation interval, emphasizing the substantial duration of maternal dependency and somatic development characteristic of this medium-sized macropodid. Sexual maturity in both sexes is marked by the onset of gonadal activity, with females entering their first oestrous cycle only after attaining this threshold body mass. The age at which puberty occurs is a key life-history parameter, as it determines the generation time and thus the potential rate of population increase under favorable environmental conditions. Interestingly, the duration of post-weaning growth until maturity is several times greater than the entire period of pouch occupancy, highlighting the importance of the juvenile and sub-adult life stages in shaping overall life-history trajectories.

Adult female swamp wallabies reach an ultimate body mass of approximately 14,625 grams [Wwi = approximately 14,625 grams], a value representing the maximum recorded wet weight for healthy individuals in the wild. This adult size, attained after a prolonged growth phase spanning several years, places the species within the medium-sized range for macropodids. The maximum reproduction rate in this species has been documented as up to 1.5 young per year [Ri = up to 1.5 young per year] at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This moderate reproductive output is typical of macropodids, which generally exhibit slow life histories characterized by small litters and extended parental care. The swamp wallaby can breed throughout the year, with no strict seasonal peak in many parts of its range. Unlike many other macropods, this species exhibits a form of embryonic diapause that allows a female to maintain a quiescent blastocyst while nursing a pouch young, ensuring rapid replacement of offspring should the current joey be lost. This reproductive strategy, combined with continuous breeding, enables females to maximize their lifetime reproductive success despite the constraints imposed by a long developmental period.

Longevity records for the swamp wallaby indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15.4 years [am = approximately 15.4 years] at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], with the oldest individuals documented in captive settings where predation is absent and nutrition is consistent. In the wild, average lifespan is considerably shorter due to predation pressure, vehicle collisions, and environmental stochasticity. Senescence in this species manifests as a gradual decline in condition, with older females showing reduced fecundity and decreased milk output during lactation. The ultimate body composition of an adult swamp wallaby includes substantial reserves of adipose tissue that are drawn upon during periods of food scarcity, particularly in drier months. Dental wear is a common indicator of age in wild populations, with molars showing progressive attrition that eventually limits the efficiency of grinding fibrous eucalypt leaves. Post-reproductive mortality typically results from starvation as tooth function declines, or from predation when weakened individuals cannot evade pursuit. These demographic patterns underscore the trade-off between current reproductive investment and somatic maintenance that shapes life-history evolution in this solitary browser.
